SKYNET

Tagline: The net that covers the world with a sky of goodness.

Who We Are
We are SKYNET—a team driven by the belief that technology is at its best when it serves humanity. Our name represents our vision: a global network that acts like the sky above us, covering the world with goodness, connection, and protection for all creation.

Our Mission
Our mission is bold but simple: To change this world into a better place for all creation by the power of technology
summary:
Hotspot is a tool that turns NASA’s two incompatible satellite fire records, MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m), into one comparable fire history for Vietnam, 2003–2026.

Joining the two records directly creates a false ×4.35 jump in 2012 and the wrong trend (+4.3% per year). We fix this by asking, for every VIIRS fire, “would MODIS Aqua have detected it on the same afternoon pass?” We model MODIS’s detection limit across its scan geometry, count fire-active 10 km cell-days, and calibrate against the 2012–2022 overlap, with 95% uncertainty bands from a bootstrap.

On held-out 2019+ data, bias falls from +318% to −6%. The 2012 step drops to ×1.08, matching Aqua, and the trend becomes −2.3% per year. The results feed seasonal calendars, anomaly flags and a dashboard for national, regional and province views.

Why it matters: local authorities can see real fire-season patterns and trends, and plan around them, instead of acting on an artifact of the sensor change.
details:
Hot Spot turns NASA’s two incompatible satellite fire records into one comparable fire history for Vietnam (2003–2026).

The problem. MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) detect fires with different sensitivity. VIIRS sees many small fires that MODIS misses, so joining the records directly creates a false ×4.35 jump in 2012 and a wrong trend (+4.3% per year), even though real fire activity changed by only ×1.08.

How it works.

  1. We clean NASA FIRMS data: afternoon passes only, UTC converted to local time (UTC+7), vegetation fires only, confidence thresholds, duplicates removed.
  2. We count fire-active 10 km cell-days instead of raw hotspots, which is far less sensitive to pixel size.
  3. For each VIIRS fire, a physical observation operator estimates whether MODIS Aqua would have detected it on the same afternoon pass. It uses a detection limit that rises with MODIS pixel size, and a logistic detection curve integrated over the scan geometry.
  4. We calibrate on the 2012–2022 overlap with a correction factor per region and calendar month, shrunk toward the national ratio.
  5. A year-block bootstrap with detection-limit scenarios gives 95% uncertainty bands.
  6. The final series uses Aqua observations to Jan 2012, then VIIRS converted to MODIS-equivalent. Aqua gap months are detected and filled automatically.

Validation. Trained on 2012–2018 and tested on 2019 onward, bias falls from +318% (raw VIIRS) to −6%, with 12% typical monthly error. The 2012 step falls from ×4.35 to ×1.08, and the trend becomes −2.3% per year (p = 0.002). A second VIIRS sensor (NOAA-20), converted with the same calibration, matches independently. Automated checks confirm that provinces sum to the national total and that bands and gaps behave.

Outputs and benefit. Province, regional and national monthly series, 10 km grids, seasonal calendars, anomaly flags and a dashboard let local managers see real fire seasons and trends, without being misled by a sensor change.

Honest limits. A hotspot is not burned area. Aqua’s orbit drifts after 2022, so we calibrate only up to 2022. FIRMS has no cloud mask.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, Matplotlib), NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS SNPP and NOAA-20), geoBoundaries, and an HTML/JavaScript dashboard.

Creative angle. We harmonize by modeling what the older sensor would have seen, not by rescaling counts.
